Lesson 037 · spatial partitioning

The city map: one structure per question

A 2 km × 2 km city, 8,000 zombies, 200 screamers and 600 buildings, on a mid-range PC at 60 fps. Three questions every frame: separation (who is within 2 m of me?), alerts (which zombies are within 60 m of a screamer?) and line of sight (can each screamer see the player past the buildings?). Budget for all three: 2.5 ms.

Lesson 053 · AI at scale

Zombie brains: who thinks, and when

5,000 zombies, each with a brain that picks a target and asks for a path: 0.003 ms a think. Far zombies can use a cheap brain (follow the horde's flow field): 0.001 ms. Budget for AI: 2 ms in every frame, and zombies next to the player react at once.

AI time, 30 frames (half a second)

Near: under 30 m. Mid: 30–100 m. Far: over 100 m, *with the cheap brain. Every: thinks once every N frames.

        Scaling test

        What this shows

        O(n²) hides in small tests

        With 500 zombies, checking everyone looks free. Each time you double the crowd, the work goes up four times, so the cost shows up suddenly.

        Measure, then fix

        The frame bar is the profiler in miniature. The separation step is the one thing to fix; the rest of the frame barely changes.

        The architect's rule

        Any "who is near me?" question goes through one shared spatial grid. Then bullets, explosions and AI senses get the same speed-up for free.

        The city map (Lesson 037) is a model, not a live timing: fine grid rebuild 0.5 ns per cell (1,000,000 cells) + 5 ns per zombie; cell visit 2 ns; distance check 4 ns; quadtree node visit 15 ns and build 20 ns per zombie per level; ray-box test 10 ns. Clumped: 6,000 zombies in a 60 × 60 m square, 2,000 spread. The screamers stand outside the square.

        Times are measured in JavaScript in your browser. A C# or C++ build will give different absolute numbers, but the same shape: about ×4 per doubling for "check everyone" and about ×2 for the grid. The frame rate cannot go above your screen's refresh rate (often 60 or 120 Hz).
